section_summary: This section follows debate over dissolving Japan’s Diet, the Kobe–Osaka riot sentences, and British views on a peace treaty and occupation policy. Later documents discuss Yoshida’s election prospects, Soviet reporting, and the fragmentation of Japan’s left wing. It ends with the opening pages of a State Department study of Japanese left-wing politics from 1918 to 1948.

subfiles.title: Diet Dissolution in 1948 Remote—Reasons for Katayama’s Advocacy of Diet Dissolution
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Assesses Katayama’s call for Diet dissolution and the Ashida Cabinet’s prospects.
subfiles.summary: Katayama favored an early election to preserve Socialist unity and future coalition cooperation. A right-wing Socialist victory made dissolution less urgent and gave the Ashida Cabinet a respite.

subfiles.title: Mr. Katayama’s Position
subfiles.about: Explains Katayama’s argument that an early election could preserve the coalition.
subfiles.summary: Editorial argues dissolution could avert a Socialist–Democratic rupture and renew the coalition’s mandate.

subfiles.summary: The editorial links the right wing’s victory to Nishio’s acquittal, Kuroda’s expulsion, and improving economic prospects.

subfiles.title: Sentences Imposed as Result of Kobe–Osaka Riots in April 1948
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards Patrick Shaw’s representation concerning sentences imposed on Korean riot defendants.
subfiles.summary: Sebald reports Shaw’s humanitarian objection to the sentences and the chief of staff’s decision to take no action.

subfiles.title: Sentences Given to Koreans Involved in Kobe Riots
subfiles.to: Chief of Staff, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Records Shaw’s request for reconsideration of sentences imposed on six Koreans.
subfiles.summary: Shaw called the sentences excessive but did not challenge the trials’ fairness.

subfiles.title: Forwarding of September 3 Memorandum of Conversation
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge of the American Mission, London
subfiles.about: Transmits Sebald’s memorandum of conversation with Sir Alvary Gascoigne.
subfiles.summary: Forwards a copy of the September 3 memorandum.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Sir Alvary Gascoigne
subfiles.about: Records British views on a Japanese peace treaty, trade, and public service labor policy.
subfiles.summary: Gascoigne said Britain hoped for an early peace conference and supported a viable Japanese economy. He described MacArthur’s sharp criticism of Australian representative Patrick Shaw over proposed public service legislation.

subfiles.title: Yoshida on a General Election
subfiles.about: Reports Yoshida’s preference for an immediate election and a strong government.
subfiles.summary: Yoshida expected an election to give him a Diet majority after resolving public service law and budget questions.

subfiles.title: Election of Yoshida, concluding page
subfiles.about: Reports a second ballot between Yoshida and Katayama.
subfiles.summary: Yoshida won the second ballot despite receiving less than a majority of votes cast.

subfiles.title: Yoshida on a General Election
subfiles.about: Repeats Yoshida’s view that Japan needs an immediate election.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of the October 22 airgram on Yoshida’s election plans.

subfiles.title: Soviet Commentary on the Ashida Cabinet Scandal
subfiles.about: Relays a Pravda account of Japanese political corruption and the Ashida Cabinet’s fall.
subfiles.summary: Reports Soviet press claims that the scandal exposed corruption throughout Japan’s ruling circles.

subfiles.title: Castle Letter to George Kennan
subfiles.about: Expresses concern that occupation policy is driving Japanese opinion toward the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Castle asks whether Kennan’s recommendations reached SCAP and warns that purges and perceived American conduct could damage support for the United States.

subfiles.title: Soviet Press Item on Takakura
subfiles.about: Reports a Soviet press item concerning a Tokyo demand for Communist Takakura’s release.
subfiles.summary: TASS cited an Akahata report of a meeting demanding Takakura’s release.

subfiles.title: Castle Letter to George Kennan
subfiles.about: Expresses concern that occupation policy is driving Japanese opinion toward the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Dated copy of Castle’s letter urging attention to purges, anti-American feeling, and Soviet influence in Japan.

subfiles.title: Left Wing Political Realignments
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Analyzes the Social Democratic Party’s fragmentation and the new Labor-Farmer Party.
subfiles.summary: The despatch describes defections from the Social Democratic Party after the public service law dispute and the founding of Kuroda’s Labor-Farmer Party. It interprets Communist interest in that party as a possible popular-front strategy and notes local Socialist–Communist mergers. Sebald warns that the weakening political center could leave conservatives facing an opposition dominated by the extreme left.

subfiles.title: Left Wing Groups in Japanese Politics, 1918–1948
subfiles.doc_type: Office of Intelligence Research report 2530A, opening pages
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Research for Far East
subfiles.about: Surveys the history and organization of Japan’s left-wing parties and labor movement.
subfiles.summary: The title page and contents outline a study of prewar proletarian parties, wartime radicals in China, postwar Socialist and Communist organizations, trade unions, and the Katayama and Ashida cabinets. The opening summary traces labor organizing under government repression and recurring divisions among social democrats, communists, and national socialists. It then describes the postwar revival of the Socialist and Communist parties and the renewed dispute over a united front. The report continues beyond page 319.
